subject: Medicine
stem: A 58-year-old man with nonischemic cardiomyopathy remains short of breath after climbing two flights of stairs. Echocardiography shows an ejection fraction of 30%. He takes sacubitril-valsartan, carvedilol, spironolactone and a stable furosemide dose. Blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg, estimated GFR is 68 mL/min/1.73 m² and hemoglobin A1c is 5.4%. He is euvolemic. Which additional medication best reduces future heart-failure events?

options.text: Sitagliptin
options.explanation: DPP-4 inhibition is used for glycemic management, but normal glycemia is not the issue and it does not provide the established HFrEF benefit.

options.text: Verapamil
options.explanation: Negative inotropy can worsen reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure; this patient needs additional disease-modifying treatment rather than a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.

options.text: Higher-dose furosemide alone
options.explanation: Loop diuretics relieve congestion, but increasing a diuretic in a euvolemic patient does not substitute for the missing disease-modifying class.

options.text: Dapagliflozin
options.explanation: SGLT2 inhibition improves outcomes in symptomatic reduced-ejection-fraction heart failure even without diabetes; his renal function and stable volume status permit consideration.

explanation: This patient has stable symptomatic HFrEF despite three major disease-modifying medication classes. An SGLT2 inhibitor completes the usual four-class foundation when no contraindication exists. Its heart-failure indication does not require diabetes or an elevated A1c. A normal glucose level therefore should not exclude treatment. Volume status, renal function and medication tolerance still require follow-up after initiation. Furosemide is useful for excess fluid rather than the missing outcome benefit; unnecessary dose escalation could cause hypovolemia. Verapamil adds a potentially harmful negative inotropic effect.
objective: Offer an SGLT2 inhibitor for symptomatic HFrEF when appropriate even when the patient does not have diabetes.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 62-year-old woman with an ejection fraction of 28% is stable on lisinopril, metoprolol succinate, spironolactone and empagliflozin. Her cardiologist plans to replace lisinopril with sacubitril-valsartan. She took her usual lisinopril this morning. Potassium is 4.4 mEq/L, blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg and she has never had angioedema. Which instruction is most appropriate for the transition?

options.text: Continue lisinopril and replace only spironolactone with sacubitril-valsartan
options.explanation: An ARNI replaces ACE-inhibitor or ARB therapy rather than being added to it; stopping the MRA does not remove the dangerous overlap.

options.text: Begin sacubitril-valsartan tonight because normal potassium eliminates transition risk
options.explanation: Normal potassium is reassuring for one toxicity but does not prevent angioedema caused by overlapping effects on vasoactive peptide metabolism.

options.text: Stop lisinopril and wait at least 36 hours before the first sacubitril-valsartan dose
options.explanation: A washout reduces overlapping ACE and neprilysin inhibition, which otherwise increases bradykinin-related angioedema risk during this medication transition.

options.text: Take both drugs together for one week and then stop lisinopril
options.explanation: Overlapping ACE inhibition with sacubitril is unsafe; gradual overlap is not needed to preserve heart-failure benefit during the transition.

explanation: Sacubitril inhibits neprilysin, and valsartan provides angiotensin receptor blockade. When replacing an ACE inhibitor, the ACE inhibitor must be stopped and an adequate washout observed before sacubitril-valsartan begins. The minimum recommended interval is 36 hours. This separation addresses angioedema risk rather than simply hyperkalemia or blood-pressure effects. Her acceptable potassium, pressure and kidney function support considering the ARNI but do not waive the interval. Existing MRA and SGLT2-inhibitor therapy can be reassessed separately according to tolerance; they are not substitutes for stopping lisinopril.
objective: Separate the last ACE-inhibitor dose from initiation of sacubitril-valsartan by at least 36 hours.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 74-year-old woman with ischemic HFrEF takes an ARNI, carvedilol, dapagliflozin and furosemide. She has mild exertional symptoms without edema. Her estimated GFR has been stable at 24 mL/min/1.73 m² for three months. Two nonhemolyzed samples show potassium of 5.3 mEq/L. A trainee proposes starting spironolactone to complete foundational therapy. Which response best addresses this proposal?

options.text: Replace dapagliflozin with spironolactone solely because she does not have diabetes
options.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors have HFrEF benefits independent of diabetes, while the proposed replacement retains the same unresolved renal and potassium safety problems.

options.text: Defer spironolactone because her renal function and potassium make initiation unsafe
options.explanation: Guideline MRA initiation requires adequate renal filtration and a lower potassium level; both current measurements increase the risk of dangerous hyperkalemia.

options.text: Start spironolactone because normal volume status prevents hyperkalemia
options.explanation: Euvolemia does not restore potassium excretion in advanced kidney disease or remove the potassium-retaining effect of mineralocorticoid receptor antagonism.

options.text: Start spironolactone and add a potassium supplement routinely
options.explanation: Adding potassium would compound an already elevated level; potassium supplementation is not a routine companion to a potassium-sparing diuretic.

explanation: An MRA can reduce HFrEF morbidity and mortality in eligible patients, but eligibility is a safety condition rather than an administrative detail. The cited heart-failure guideline recommends initiation when estimated GFR exceeds 30 mL/min/1.73 m² and potassium is below 5.0 mEq/L. This patient fails both criteria. Her lack of edema does not protect against hyperkalemia. The appropriate response is to defer initiation, review reversible contributors to the potassium elevation and coordinate renal and heart-failure management. Completing a medication checklist cannot justify exposing her to a foreseeable serious adverse effect.
objective: Check renal function and potassium before initiating an MRA for HFrEF; benefits do not override unsafe starting values.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 45-year-old man developed dilated cardiomyopathy two years ago. His ejection fraction rose from 25% to 56% while taking carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. He has been asymptomatic for nine months and no longer needs a loop diuretic. Kidney function and potassium are normal. He asks to stop all heart medications because his latest echocardiogram is normal. What is the best recommendation?

options.text: Continue disease-modifying heart-failure therapy if tolerated
options.explanation: Improved ejection fraction reflects remission on therapy and does not reliably identify a patient who can stop treatment without recurrent ventricular dysfunction.

options.text: Stop all drugs now and restart only if ankle swelling returns
options.explanation: Clinical congestion can appear after ventricular relapse; waiting for edema sacrifices preventive treatment and may miss earlier deterioration in cardiac function.

options.text: Stop the ARNI but retain only an as-needed loop diuretic
options.explanation: A loop diuretic treats fluid retention and does not replace neurohormonal therapy that helped produce and maintain ventricular recovery in this patient.

options.text: Substitute verapamil because recovered ejection fraction requires a different drug class
options.explanation: Recovery does not create a new indication for verapamil, and replacing proven therapy with a negative inotrope lacks an appropriate rationale.

explanation: This is heart failure with improved ejection fraction. Normalization of the measured ejection fraction during therapy should not be interpreted as proof that the cardiomyopathy has permanently disappeared. Relapse after withdrawal is a recognized concern, so disease-modifying treatment should generally continue if tolerated. The loop diuretic can be adjusted to congestion, explaining why he no longer needs it, but that does not establish that the other medications are unnecessary. Discuss burden and adverse effects explicitly, then individualize dosing rather than discontinuing the entire preventive regimen because one imaging measurement improved.
objective: Continue tolerated HFrEF disease-modifying treatment after ejection fraction improves to reduce relapse risk.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 59-year-old woman with an ejection fraction of 32% has persistent fatigue despite stable optimized heart-failure treatment. She is euvolemic and reports no chest pain. Hemoglobin is 12.3 g/dL, ferritin is 145 ng/mL and transferrin saturation is 14%. C-reactive protein is mildly elevated. Thyroid function is normal. Which interpretation of her iron studies is most appropriate?

options.text: Iron deficiency is excluded because hemoglobin is above 12 g/dL
options.explanation: Iron deficiency can impair function before overt anemia develops; hemoglobin alone does not assess tissue iron availability in chronic heart failure.

options.text: Iron overload is established because ferritin exceeds 100 ng/mL
options.explanation: Ferritin can rise with inflammation, and this modest value with low transferrin saturation does not establish excess body iron stores.

options.text: The low transferrin saturation proves active gastrointestinal hemorrhage
options.explanation: Low iron availability warrants assessment of causes, but it cannot independently localize a bleeding source or establish ongoing blood loss.

options.text: Iron deficiency relevant to heart failure remains present despite the nonlow ferritin
options.explanation: In symptomatic heart failure, ferritin between 100 and 300 ng/mL with transferrin saturation below 20% can identify deficient available iron.

explanation: Iron deficiency in heart failure is not restricted to patients with severe anemia or a frankly low ferritin. Ferritin is influenced by inflammation, so transferrin saturation helps identify reduced iron availability when ferritin is in an intermediate range. Her ferritin of 145 ng/mL and saturation of 14% fit the commonly used heart-failure trial and guideline definition. This finding warrants assessment of cause and discussion of appropriate replacement; it does not prove hemorrhage or iron overload. The question tests interpretation rather than a specific iron formulation or infusion schedule.
objective: Use ferritin together with transferrin saturation to recognize iron deficiency in heart failure even without marked anemia.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 41-year-old man has eaten mainly sweetened tea and small amounts of white rice for four months after losing his housing. He has burning feet, leg edema, tachycardia and warm extremities. Echocardiography shows a hyperdynamic ventricle without valvular disease. Lactate is 5.0 mmol/L despite normal oxygenation and no evidence of infection. Hemoglobin and thyroid studies are normal. Which nutritional disorder best unifies these findings?

options.text: Vitamin C deficiency causing scurvy
options.explanation: Scurvy produces impaired connective-tissue integrity, gingival disease and bleeding; it does not best explain this combined metabolic and circulatory pattern.

options.text: Vitamin A deficiency causing impaired epithelial differentiation
options.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency primarily produces ocular and epithelial findings, not the paired neuropathy and high-output heart-failure phenotype described here.

options.text: Thiamin deficiency causing wet beriberi
options.explanation: Severe thiamin depletion can combine peripheral neuropathy, impaired oxidative metabolism and high-output cardiac failure after a prolonged nutritionally restricted diet.

options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency causing megaloblastic anemia
options.explanation: B12 deficiency can cause neuropathy, but normal hemoglobin and high-output failure with lactic acidosis are less consistent with its usual presentation.

explanation: Thiamin is essential to carbohydrate oxidative metabolism. Prolonged deficient intake can cause neuropathy and cardiovascular beriberi, including vasodilation, high-output physiology and edema. Impaired oxidation also provides a coherent explanation for lactate accumulation despite adequate oxygenation. The vignette excludes severe anemia and hyperthyroidism, two other high-output causes, and provides no infection evidence. Early recognition matters because replacement is time sensitive; nutritional rehabilitation should address other deficiencies as well. An empiric treatment response can support the clinical impression, but the diagnosis should not depend on delaying replacement while waiting for a specialized assay.
objective: Consider cardiovascular thiamin deficiency when malnutrition, neuropathy, lactic acidosis and high-output failure occur together.
keyPoints: Consider cardiovascular thiamin deficiency when malnutrition, neuropathy, lactic acidosis and high-output failure occur together.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 47-year-old woman with confirmed hypertension wants a practical dietary change alongside her prescribed medication. Kidney function and potassium are normal. She usually eats processed meat sandwiches, chips and sweetened drinks, with few vegetables. She does not want to purchase supplements. She cooks at home most evenings. Which proposed eating pattern most closely follows an evidence-based blood-pressure-lowering approach for her?

options.text: Replace all meals with fruit juice and avoid protein-containing foods
options.explanation: Juice-only intake is nutritionally unbalanced and does not provide the fiber, protein variety or overall food pattern used in DASH.

options.text: Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes and low-fat dairy with reduced sodium
options.explanation: This combination follows the DASH pattern and addresses both food quality and sodium exposure without requiring commercial supplements or a specialized product.

options.text: Processed meat and full-fat cheese as long as carbohydrate intake is very low
options.explanation: Restricting carbohydrates does not neutralize the sodium and saturated-fat burden of the proposed foods or make this pattern equivalent to DASH.

options.text: Continue the same foods and add a high-dose vitamin E capsule
options.explanation: An isolated antioxidant supplement does not reproduce the blood-pressure benefit of the dietary pattern and leaves the major sodium sources unchanged.

explanation: DASH is a flexible food pattern rather than a branded supplement program. It emphasizes vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes and appropriate low-fat dairy while limiting sodium and foods high in saturated fat. The patient has no stated renal or potassium restriction that would require modifying these choices. Medication and dietary treatment can be used together. A sustainable plan might begin with replacing processed lunch foods and sweetened drinks rather than prescribing a rigid menu. Vitamin supplementation alone and severe exclusion diets do not reproduce this overall nutritional intervention.
objective: Recommend a DASH-style food pattern with lower sodium as part of hypertension treatment when individual nutritional restrictions do not preclude it.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 69-year-old man with hypertension brings his usual lunch to a dietitian visit. He avoids adding table salt and therefore believes his sodium intake is low. The soup label lists 650 mg sodium per serving and two servings per container; he eats the entire container. His sandwich contains 700 mg sodium. Which counseling statement most accurately identifies the sodium exposure from this lunch?

options.text: The lunch supplies 2,000 mg sodium before any other meals or snacks
options.explanation: The entire soup container contributes 1,300 mg, which must be added to the 700 mg sandwich rather than counted as one serving.

options.text: The lunch supplies 1,350 mg because a container always counts as one serving
options.explanation: This ignores the two labeled servings in the soup container and underestimates the sodium he actually consumes at lunch.

options.text: The sodium content is negligible because he does not use a salt shaker
options.explanation: Packaged and restaurant foods can supply substantial sodium even when a patient adds no salt during preparation or at the table.

options.text: Only the sandwich sodium counts because sodium in liquids is not absorbed
options.explanation: Sodium in soup is absorbed and contributes to daily intake; a food being liquid does not exempt it from sodium accounting.

explanation: The relevant exposure is the amount eaten, not the number printed beside a single labeled serving. Two soup servings provide 1,300 mg of sodium, and the sandwich adds another 700 mg, for a total of 2,000 mg. That is already a substantial part of an entire day of sodium intake. Avoiding the salt shaker is helpful but does not address these processed-food sources. Counseling should use the label calculation to identify feasible lower-sodium substitutions rather than simply repeat a vague instruction to eat less salt or assume nonadherence.
objective: Calculate sodium intake from the number of servings actually eaten and include packaged-food sodium in hypertension counseling.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 56-year-old woman is attending rehabilitation after an uncomplicated myocardial infarction. She takes a high-intensity statin and has stopped smoking. She cooks most meals in butter and wants a single useful change to her usual meals. Her weight is stable and she has no food allergy. Which substitution best supports secondary cardiovascular prevention without simply adding extra calories?

options.text: Add olive oil to every meal while leaving the butter amount unchanged
options.explanation: Adding an energy-dense food without replacing the saturated-fat source does not accomplish the intended substitution and can increase total caloric intake.

options.text: Replace butter calories primarily with sweetened beverages
options.explanation: Refined sugar is not an appropriate replacement strategy for cardiovascular prevention and can worsen dietary quality and triglyceride-related risk.

options.text: Stop all dietary fat and rely on refined bread for most calories
options.explanation: An extreme low-fat pattern dominated by refined carbohydrate is not the recommended secondary-prevention food pattern and excludes useful unsaturated-fat sources.

options.text: Use an appropriate amount of olive oil instead of butter when preparing meals
options.explanation: Replacing a saturated-fat source with an unsaturated-fat source improves the fat pattern; substituting rather than adding also avoids unnecessary extra energy intake.

explanation: The decision concerns replacement, not whether any single food can erase established coronary risk. A Mediterranean-style pattern uses unsaturated fats in place of saturated-fat sources while also emphasizing plant foods and appropriate protein. Replacing butter with a measured amount of olive oil fits that principle. Adding oil to unchanged meals is a different intervention and can increase energy intake. Replacing fat mainly with refined starch or sugar does not supply the same dietary-quality improvement. Nutrition remains an adjunct to statin therapy, rehabilitation and other indicated secondary-prevention measures rather than a reason to stop them.
objective: For secondary coronary prevention, replace saturated-fat sources with unsaturated-fat sources within a sustainable overall food pattern.

stem: A 70-year-old man with prior coronary stenting takes atorvastatin and indicated antiplatelet therapy. A friend recommends replacing both with nonprescription fish-oil capsules and high-dose antioxidant vitamins. He has no medication intolerance, bleeding or other reason to change treatment. His fasting lipid levels are controlled on treatment. He asks whether natural products provide equivalent protection. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Replace antiplatelet therapy because antioxidant vitamins prevent stent thrombosis
options.explanation: Antioxidant vitamins have no established role as a substitute for indicated antiplatelet treatment and do not reliably prevent platelet-mediated stent thrombosis.

options.text: Take supplements only on days when prescribed medications are omitted
options.explanation: Alternating unproven supplements with indicated treatment creates treatment gaps without providing an evidence-based strategy for reducing coronary events.

options.text: Continue indicated medications; these supplements are not equivalent substitutes for event prevention
options.explanation: Nonprescription fish oil and antioxidant vitamins do not replace proven coronary secondary-prevention therapies, and a supplement label does not establish equivalent clinical outcomes.

options.text: Replace the statin because all fish-oil products have the same evidence as prescription agents
options.explanation: Over-the-counter preparations differ from studied prescription therapies, and neither a generic fish-oil claim nor omega-3 content establishes statin-equivalent benefit.

explanation: Established coronary disease requires therapies with demonstrated clinical benefit and a treatment plan matched to bleeding risk and time since intervention. Nonprescription fish oil and antioxidant vitamins should not be treated as interchangeable with statins or antiplatelet drugs. Prescription agents studied for selected indications are a separate question and do not validate all retail formulations. Explain the distinction without dismissing the patient’s interest in nutrition: food-pattern changes can complement medication, whereas replacing effective treatment with these products leaves preventable risk unaddressed. Review cost, pill burden and the specific reason he wants to switch.
objective: Do not substitute nonprescription fish-oil or antioxidant supplements for indicated coronary secondary-prevention medication.

stem: A 53-year-old woman has persistent atrial fibrillation and a mechanical mitral valve implanted five years ago. She takes warfarin and has reliable INR follow-up. She has had no bleeding or thromboembolic event. After seeing an advertisement, she asks to switch to apixaban because it does not require INR testing. Renal and hepatic function are normal. Which recommendation is most appropriate?

options.text: Stop anticoagulation if a clinic ECG shows sinus rhythm
options.explanation: The mechanical valve independently requires anticoagulation regardless of whether AF is captured on a particular visit or a rhythm-control procedure succeeds.

options.text: Continue a vitamin K antagonist for the mechanical valve
options.explanation: Mechanical prosthetic valves require vitamin K antagonist anticoagulation; normal kidney function does not make a direct oral anticoagulant an appropriate substitute.

options.text: Switch to apixaban because all patients with AF are eligible
options.explanation: The usual DOAC preference in atrial fibrillation excludes mechanical valves, so the rhythm diagnosis cannot override the prosthesis-specific requirement.

options.text: Use aspirin alone because the valve was implanted more than a year ago
options.explanation: A mature mechanical prosthesis remains thrombogenic; time since surgery does not remove the need for appropriate long-term systemic anticoagulation.

explanation: The indication for anticoagulation here is not limited to atrial fibrillation. A mechanical mitral prosthesis has its own continuing thromboembolic risk and requires a vitamin K antagonist. Direct oral anticoagulants are not suitable replacements for this indication even when kidney and liver function are normal. Discuss ways to reduce INR-monitoring burden while maintaining the correct drug class. Aspirin alone is insufficient, and an apparently normal rhythm does not change the prosthesis-related requirement. Any target INR and adjunctive therapy should be checked against valve type and current specialist guidance.
objective: Use a vitamin K antagonist rather than a DOAC in a patient with a mechanical prosthetic valve.

stem: A 49-year-old man has recurrent symptomatic atrial fibrillation despite an otherwise appropriate rhythm-control plan. He drinks four beers nightly and often six drinks on weekends. Thyroid function and electrolytes are normal. He asks what lifestyle change could reduce arrhythmia recurrence. He is willing to change his drinking and has no history suggesting alcohol withdrawal. Which recommendation best addresses his stated goal?

options.text: Minimize or eliminate alcohol consumption as part of the rhythm-control plan
options.explanation: Alcohol reduction can reduce AF recurrence and burden; addressing his substantial exposure complements treatment rather than replacing indicated stroke prevention or rhythm management.

options.text: Change beer to liquor while keeping the same number of standard drinks
options.explanation: Ethanol exposure rather than the beverage label is the relevant concern; switching beverage type without reducing standard drinks does not address it.

subject: Pediatrics
stem: A 14-year-old girl has no exertional symptoms and a normal cardiovascular examination. Her father was recently diagnosed with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and testing identified a pathogenic sarcomere-gene variant. Her mother asks whether a normal school sports examination excludes disease. The girl has not had cardiac imaging or genetic counseling. No family member has received counseling previously. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure the family that an absent murmur excludes inherited HCM
options.explanation: HCM can be clinically silent and may not produce resting outflow obstruction; auscultation alone cannot rule out an inherited predisposition.

options.text: Wait until she develops syncope before performing any cardiac evaluation
options.explanation: Symptom-triggered testing alone misses presymptomatic relatives and delays appropriate surveillance in a child with an established first-degree familial risk.

options.text: Implant a defibrillator immediately based only on her father’s genetic result

options.explanation: A first-degree relative can carry the familial pathogenic variant before hypertrophy or symptoms appear; a normal examination does not replace cascade assessment.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 35-year-old woman with established hypertrophic cardiomyopathy reports exertional chest pressure and near-syncope while walking uphill. Resting echocardiography shows asymmetric septal thickening, systolic anterior mitral motion and an outflow gradient of 18 mm Hg. A Valsalva maneuver does not produce a significant gradient. No sustained arrhythmia is captured during symptoms. Which study best assesses whether dynamic obstruction contributes during exertion?

options.text: A coronary calcium score as a direct measure of outflow obstruction
options.explanation: Coronary calcium estimates atherosclerotic burden and cannot measure the exertion-dependent pressure gradient across the left ventricular outflow tract.

options.text: A resting chest radiograph to quantify the septal pressure gradient
options.explanation: Radiography may show heart size or pulmonary findings, but it does not provide the Doppler hemodynamic measurement needed for this question.

options.text: Exercise echocardiography to assess a provocable outflow gradient
options.explanation: Exercise can uncover dynamic LV outflow obstruction not evident at rest or with a simple provocation, connecting the measurement to her symptom trigger.

subject: Surgery
stem: A 72-year-old woman is scheduled for cataract surgery under local anesthesia. She had coronary stenting six years ago and has had no angina, dyspnea or syncope since then. She walks briskly for thirty minutes and climbs two flights of stairs without symptoms. Her examination is unchanged. The surgical office requests a stress test solely because she has a coronary history. What is the most appropriate cardiac-testing plan?

options.text: Proceed without routine preoperative stress testing
options.explanation: Low-risk surgery in an asymptomatic patient with good functional capacity does not justify stress testing solely for a remote coronary diagnosis.

options.text: Obtain invasive coronary angiography before allowing any elective procedure
options.explanation: Angiography is not a routine prerequisite for low-risk surgery and exposes this stable patient to an invasive procedure without an independent indication.

options.text: Perform stress testing because age above 70 is an absolute indication
options.explanation: Age contributes to clinical context but does not by itself override a low-risk procedure and reassuring functional status in the stepwise evaluation.

stem: A 59-year-old man with coronary disease presents with chest pressure. He is hemodynamically stable, and the team is beginning an acute coronary evaluation. Before nitroglycerin is administered, he reports taking sildenafil two hours earlier. He has not received a nitrate. Which medication action is most appropriate while the rest of his evaluation and indicated treatment proceed?

options.text: Withhold nitrates because recent sildenafil can markedly potentiate hypotension
options.explanation: Sildenafil and nitrates both amplify the nitric oxide–cGMP vasodilator pathway; their close coadministration can cause a clinically dangerous blood-pressure drop.

options.text: Give a larger nitroglycerin dose because sildenafil blocks its effect
options.explanation: Sildenafil potentiates rather than blocks nitrate-mediated vasodilation, so increasing the nitrate dose would intensify the interaction rather than overcome resistance.

options.text: Cancel the acute coronary evaluation because sildenafil explains every possible cause of pain
options.explanation: A drug-interaction history changes medication selection but does not exclude an acute coronary syndrome or remove the need to evaluate ongoing chest symptoms.

options.text: Use a long-acting nitrate immediately because only sublingual formulations interact
options.explanation: The interaction concerns nitrate pharmacology rather than a single route; a long-acting preparation does not avoid the same hazardous vasodilator combination.

explanation: The medication history changes the safety of a commonly used symptom treatment. Sildenafil inhibits phosphodiesterase-5 and can greatly potentiate nitrate-related cGMP effects, causing severe hypotension. Nitrates should therefore be withheld after the recent dose while the team continues the appropriate chest-pain evaluation and other indicated treatment. This is not evidence that the pain is benign or that all coronary care must stop. Both short- and long-acting nitrate formulations are relevant. The vignette uses a clearly recent exposure rather than testing a borderline timing decision that would require additional drug and patient-specific considerations.
objective: Avoid nitrate administration after recent sildenafil exposure because of the risk of profound hypotension.

stem: A 34-year-old woman has a first episode of clinically diagnosed acute idiopathic pericarditis. She is stable, with a small effusion and no tamponade, myocardial dysfunction, immunosuppression or fever. Kidney and liver function are normal, pregnancy testing is negative and she has no relevant interacting medication. She begins an appropriate NSAID with gastroprotection. Which adjunctive medication is generally recommended to improve disease control and reduce recurrence?

options.text: Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for every idiopathic episode

stem: A 63-year-old man had PCI for stable coronary disease three years ago. He has no angina, breathlessness or decline in exercise tolerance. subject: Medicine
stem: A 66-year-old woman with HFrEF develops increased edema after a week of high-sodium prepared meals while visiting family. Her serum sodium remains 139 mEq/L. Her loop diuretic dose has remained unchanged throughout the trip. She asks how salt could contribute when the sodium concentration in her blood is normal. Which explanation best reconciles the normal concentration with her fluid retention?

options.text: Only a sodium concentration above 160 mEq/L can be associated with heart-failure congestion
options.explanation: Congestion can occur across a range of serum sodium values, including normal or low levels; extreme hypernatremia is not a prerequisite.

options.text: Serum sodium reflects a concentration, while retained total-body sodium can expand extracellular volume with accompanying water
options.explanation: Water retention can accompany retained sodium so that the measured concentration stays near normal even as extracellular volume and congestive symptoms increase.

options.text: A normal sodium concentration proves that total-body sodium and extracellular volume are unchanged
options.explanation: Concentration is not the same as total content; proportional changes in sodium and water can preserve the laboratory value while expanding volume.

options.text: Dietary sodium can enter only the intracellular compartment and therefore cannot influence edema
options.explanation: Sodium is a major extracellular solute, and the proposed exclusive intracellular distribution is incompatible with its role in extracellular fluid balance.

explanation: Serum sodium is a ratio related to body solute and water balance, not a direct inventory of total-body sodium. In a patient predisposed to retain salt and water, increased total sodium can be accompanied by sufficient water to keep the serum concentration normal while extracellular volume rises. This distinction explains why a normal concentration does not refute clinically evident edema and venous congestion. Her dietary exposure should be considered alongside medications, kidney function and other causes of worsening. The answer does not assume that a precise universal sodium limit or dietary blame alone can resolve every episode of heart failure.
objective: Distinguish normal serum sodium concentration from increased total-body sodium and extracellular volume in congestive heart failure.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has genetically confirmed lipoprotein lipase deficiency with recurrent pancreatitis and extreme fasting hypertriglyceridemia. Her lipid specialist and dietitian are designing a nutritionally adequate plan with marked long-chain-fat restriction. She asks why both animal fats and many vegetable oils must be counted. Which explanation best links the food restriction to her metabolic defect?

options.text: Long-chain dietary fats are packaged into intestinal chylomicrons whose triglyceride clearance depends on the impaired LPL pathway
options.explanation: Both animal and vegetable long-chain fats can contribute to chylomicron production, so plant origin alone does not bypass the deficient triglyceride-clearance mechanism.

options.text: Only animal fat enters chylomicrons, while every vegetable oil enters directly through the portal vein
options.explanation: Plant origin does not determine complete avoidance of chylomicron packaging; many vegetable oils contain long-chain fatty acids using the same transport pathway.

options.text: LPL deficiency prevents dietary fat absorption and therefore eliminates any need for fat restriction
options.explanation: The central defect is impaired clearance of triglyceride-rich particles after absorption, not a protective inability to absorb and package dietary fat.

options.text: Dietary fat restriction works solely by directly stimulating hepatic LDL receptors
options.explanation: LDL receptor activity does not explain the specific reduction in chylomicron substrate load sought in this severe LPL-dependent triglyceride disorder.

explanation: Long-chain dietary fatty acids are incorporated into triglycerides and transported in chylomicrons. Lipoprotein lipase is important for hydrolysis and clearance of their triglyceride cargo. In severe deficiency, reducing the long-chain dietary-fat load reduces input into a pathway with markedly impaired clearance. Both animal and many plant oils use this route; an oil being plant-derived is not enough to make it unrestricted. Specialized dietary planning must still preserve nutritional adequacy and essential fatty-acid requirements. This item tests substrate handling rather than an exact gram limit or a claim that diet is the only available treatment.
objective: Explain why long-chain fat from both animal and plant sources contributes to chylomicron accumulation in lipoprotein lipase deficiency.

stem: A 42-year-old woman has progressive dyspnea, tachycardia and leg edema. She has heavy menstrual bleeding and has eaten little iron-containing food for months. Hemoglobin is 4.8 g/dL, MCV is 61 fL and ferritin is 3 ng/mL. Echocardiography shows a hyperdynamic ventricle without structural valve disease. Thyroid testing is normal. Which diagnosis best explains the combined hematologic and circulatory findings?

options.text: Iron overload cardiomyopathy
options.explanation: Very low ferritin and microcytosis support depleted rather than excessive iron, while iron-overload cardiomyopathy would require an entirely different biochemical context.

options.text: Primary hypothyroid cardiomyopathy as the best explanation
options.explanation: Normal thyroid testing and a hyperdynamic circulation do not support hypothyroidism, and that diagnosis would not explain the profound iron-depleted microcytic anemia.

options.text: An isolated dietary sodium excess without a hematologic contribution
options.explanation: Sodium intake alone cannot explain hemoglobin of 4.8 g/dL, marked microcytosis and depleted ferritin; the severe oxygen-carrying deficit is clinically central.

options.text: Profound iron-deficiency anemia with high-output circulatory stress
options.explanation: Marked microcytic anemia with depleted ferritin establishes iron deficiency, and severe loss of oxygen-carrying capacity can drive a hyperdynamic circulatory response with congestion.

explanation: The iron indices and microcytosis indicate severe iron-deficiency anemia. At this degree of anemia, reduced oxygen delivery can produce tachycardia and increased cardiac output, potentially culminating in congestion even without a primary structural valve lesion. Heavy bleeding and inadequate intake both deserve investigation rather than treating dietary history as the only cause. The immediate severity requires monitored clinical management, and the question does not specify a transfusion or replacement regimen without the complete assessment. Iron overload is inconsistent with the measured stores, and an otherwise normal hyperdynamic ventricle does not make the profound anemia incidental.
objective: Recognize profound iron-deficiency anemia as a potential cause of high-output cardiovascular stress while investigating both intake and blood loss.

stem: A 51-year-old man with chronic severe aortic regurgitation has blood pressure of 164/48 mm Hg and bounding peripheral pulses. He is not febrile or anemic. His rhythm is regular at 76/min without signs of shock. Echocardiography shows left ventricular volume enlargement and substantial diastolic regurgitant flow through the aortic valve. Which mechanism best explains the unusually wide pulse pressure?

options.text: Complete absence of left ventricular stroke volume
options.explanation: Absent stroke volume would be incompatible with the bounding pulses and preserved systemic perfusion; chronic regurgitation instead creates a high total ejected volume.

options.text: Aortic outflow obstruction that prevents any diastolic return flow
options.explanation: The imaging establishes regurgitant diastolic flow, not a purely obstructive lesion; blocking that return cannot explain the stated hemodynamics.

options.text: Increased systolic ejection combined with diastolic runoff back into the left ventricle
options.explanation: A larger total stroke volume can raise systolic pressure while regurgitant diastolic runoff lowers aortic diastolic pressure, widening the pulse-pressure difference.

options.text: Equal elevation of systolic and diastolic pressure from isolated volume loss
options.explanation: Volume loss does not explain the supplied regurgitant physiology, and equal increases in both pressures would not account for a wider difference.

explanation: In chronic AR, the left ventricle handles both normal pulmonary venous inflow and blood returning through the incompetent aortic valve. The enlarged total systolic ejection can increase systolic pressure. During diastole, additional runoff from the aorta back into the ventricle reduces diastolic aortic pressure. Together these changes can widen pulse pressure and produce bounding pulses. The precise pressure pattern depends on severity, vascular properties and adaptation, so it should not be treated as a stand-alone severity measurement. The echo findings supply the established lesion whose physiology the question asks the learner to explain.
objective: Explain widened pulse pressure in chronic AR through increased total systolic ejection and aortic diastolic runoff.
keyPoints: Explain widened pulse pressure in chronic AR through increased total systolic ejection and aortic diastolic runoff.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 60-year-old woman has chronic severe primary mitral regurgitation, reduced exercise tolerance and an ejection fraction of 61%. The left ventricle is enlarged compared with the prior study. A trainee concludes that her forward cardiac output and intrinsic contractility must be normal because the ejection fraction exceeds 60%. Which physiological principle best explains why that conclusion is unsafe?

options.text: Mitral regurgitation causes a fixed obstruction preventing any ventricular emptying
options.explanation: Regurgitation creates an additional ejection pathway into the atrium rather than a fixed blockage of all systolic emptying from the ventricle.

options.text: Measured ejection includes blood entering the low-pressure left atrium as well as blood ejected into the aorta
options.explanation: Total LV emptying can appear preserved when part of the stroke volume is regurgitant; forward output and myocardial function cannot be inferred from EF alone.

options.text: Ejection fraction directly measures only aortic forward flow and excludes every regurgitant component
options.explanation: The usual chamber-volume ejection fraction describes total ventricular emptying, so it does not inherently separate forward aortic volume from mitral regurgitant volume.

options.text: An ejection fraction above 60% makes all severe mitral regurgitation measurements erroneous
options.explanation: A substantial regurgitant lesion can coexist with a seemingly preserved EF; that value does not invalidate independent anatomical or Doppler evidence of severity.

explanation: A volume-derived EF is the fraction of end-diastolic volume leaving the ventricle during systole. In MR, that total includes both effective forward flow and regurgitant flow into the atrium. The lower-impedance regurgitant pathway also changes loading conditions, so apparent preservation of EF may conceal emerging myocardial dysfunction. Interpretation therefore needs lesion severity, ventricular dimensions, symptoms and forward hemodynamics, not one fraction alone. The vignette does not use a particular value to select surgery automatically; it challenges the unsupported inference that an apparently normal total ejection fraction guarantees normal forward performance.
objective: Distinguish total ventricular ejection fraction from effective forward flow when interpreting severe mitral regurgitation.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 57-year-old man on hemodialysis develops progressive congestion after enlargement of a high-flow arm arteriovenous fistula. Hemodynamic evaluation shows high cardiac output and reduced systemic vascular resistance. Temporary supervised compression of the access decreases output. There is no severe anemia, hyperthyroidism or sepsis. Dialysis weights and ultrafiltration records have been reviewed without another sufficient explanation. Which mechanism best explains the fistula’s contribution?

options.text: A low-resistance arteriovenous shunt increases venous return and the sustained cardiac workload
options.explanation: Direct arterial-to-venous flow bypasses part of the resistance circulation, increasing return and required output; a large chronic burden can overwhelm cardiac reserve.

options.text: The fistula directly blocks all pulmonary venous return
options.explanation: An arm AV connection does not anatomically occlude pulmonary veins and would not explain the high output and response to access compression.

options.text: The fistula causes high output solely by permanently closing the aortic valve
options.explanation: Aortic valve closure would prevent systemic ejection rather than produce the measured high-output state and does not follow from an upper-limb AV connection.

options.text: High cardiac output excludes heart failure regardless of filling pressures or symptoms
options.explanation: Heart failure describes an inability to meet physiological needs without abnormal pressures; high measured output does not preclude congestion and inadequate circulatory adaptation.

explanation: An arteriovenous fistula supplies a low-resistance pathway that bypasses the usual arteriolar bed. A sufficiently large shunt increases venous return and the output required to sustain the circulation. If cardiac reserve cannot accommodate the persistent burden, congestion and high-output heart failure can develop. The measured response to supervised compression supports a causal contribution from the access rather than proving that every dialysis fistula requires intervention. Management must balance cardiovascular effects with dialysis-access needs. This is not ordinary low-output systolic failure, and the high output should not be used to dismiss clinically important filling-pressure elevation.
objective: Explain high-output failure from a large AV fistula as sustained low-resistance shunting with increased venous return and cardiac workload.

subject: Pediatrics
stem: A 15-year-old boy has brief loss of consciousness while swimming, followed by rapid recovery. He had a similar episode during running six months ago. An uncle died suddenly at age 24. Repeated ECGs after stabilization show a QTc of 520 ms. Potassium, calcium and magnesium are normal, and he takes no medication or supplement known to prolong repolarization. Which diagnosis requires priority evaluation?

options.text: Simple vasovagal syncope proven solely by brief recovery time
options.explanation: Rapid recovery can follow arrhythmic syncope; the prolonged QTc and family history are warning findings that cannot be dismissed as a routine vasovagal episode.

options.text: Epilepsy established by every transient loss of consciousness
options.explanation: Loss of consciousness alone does not establish epilepsy, especially when exertional triggers and an objective cardiac repolarization abnormality provide a competing explanation.

options.text: Normal adolescent ECG variation requiring no follow-up
options.explanation: A repeatedly measured QTc of 520 ms with concerning symptoms and family history is not adequately explained as ordinary physiological adolescent variation.

options.text: Congenital long QT syndrome
options.explanation: Repeated substantial QTc prolongation, exertional syncope and young sudden death in the family support an inherited repolarization disorder after common acquired causes are assessed.

explanation: The ECG finding becomes clinically meaningful in the context of exertional collapse and a family history of young sudden death. Long QT syndrome can predispose to dangerous ventricular rhythms and warrants prompt specialist evaluation. Normal electrolytes and the absence of relevant exposures reduce common acquired explanations but do not by themselves prove a particular genotype. An appropriate assessment includes accurate interval measurement and clinical criteria rather than relying on one automated reading. Brief recovery does not distinguish benign from arrhythmic syncope. This presentation should therefore not be labeled epilepsy or vasovagal syncope without addressing the cardiac warning signs.
objective: Prioritize inherited long QT evaluation when recurrent exertional syncope accompanies persistent marked QTc prolongation and a family history of sudden death.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 29-year-old endurance cyclist undergoes ECG recording after an incidental irregular pulse. During a resting strip, successive PR intervals lengthen from 180 to 220 to 260 ms before a P wave fails to conduct. The next conducted beat has a PR interval of 180 ms, and the sequence repeats. QRS complexes are narrow. He has no exertional symptoms. Which rhythm pattern is demonstrated?

options.text: Complete AV block
options.explanation: Complete block produces AV dissociation rather than repeated sequences of conducted P waves with predictable PR progression before an isolated nonconducted beat.

options.text: Atrial fibrillation
options.explanation: AF lacks organized repeating P waves and this patterned AV conduction sequence; an irregular pulse by itself is insufficient to assign the rhythm.

options.text: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz I pattern
options.explanation: Progressive PR prolongation followed by a nonconducted P wave and resetting of the PR interval is the defining Wenckebach sequence illustrated here.

options.text: Second-degree AV block, Mobitz II pattern
options.explanation: Mobitz II has intermittent nonconduction without the progressive PR lengthening described; labeling every dropped beat Mobitz II ignores the sequential interval evidence.

explanation: The sequence, not simply the dropped beat, identifies this as a Mobitz I or Wenckebach pattern. Progressive nodal delay lengthens the PR interval until an atrial impulse is not conducted, followed by a reset. Narrow QRS complexes and the resting athletic context are compatible with a nodal or physiological contribution, but interpretation still requires medication, symptom and clinical review. The question identifies the demonstrated rhythm rather than declaring that every such patient needs no evaluation. It differs from acquired Mobitz II, where the pattern and progression risk lead to a different pacing discussion.
objective: Identify Mobitz I AV block from progressive PR prolongation followed by nonconduction and resetting of the PR interval.

stem: A 45-year-old woman has recurrent chest pain at rest around dawn but can walk uphill during the day without symptoms. During an observed episode, ECG shows transient inferior ST elevation. stem: A 73-year-old woman has abrupt severe back pain and hypertension. Noncontrast CT shows a crescent of high attenuation within the descending thoracic aortic wall. stem: A 55-year-old man has a severe headache, confusion and blood pressure of 238/142 mm Hg. Examination shows bilateral optic-disc swelling without a focal neurological deficit. stem: A 32-year-old woman develops progressive orthopnea and ankle edema five weeks after an uncomplicated delivery. She had no known cardiac disease before pregnancy. options.explanation: Athletic adaptation does not explain new symptomatic low-ejection-fraction failure after delivery in a patient without a corresponding training history or alternative benign explanation.

options.explanation: New otherwise unexplained systolic failure arising near pregnancy or after delivery in a previously unaffected patient fits the clinical definition of peripartum cardiomyopathy.

options.explanation: Orthopnea, venous congestion and an ejection fraction of 29% exceed ordinary postpartum fluid changes and establish clinically important ventricular dysfunction.

options.text: Isolated lower-extremity venous insufficiency
options.explanation: Venous disease can cause dependent edema but does not explain pulmonary congestion, elevated jugular pressure and global left ventricular systolic failure.

explanation: Peripartum cardiomyopathy is considered when heart failure with reduced systolic function develops toward the end of pregnancy or in the postpartum period without another identifiable cause. Her timing, objective congestion and markedly reduced ejection fraction fit that pattern. Because the diagnosis is one of exclusion, the alternative cardiac and noncardiac causes in the vignette matter. Mild postpartum swelling should not be used to dismiss orthopnea or pulmonary congestion. The case tests recognition, not a treatment regimen; management needs a coordinated team and consideration of lactation, hemodynamic severity and other individual factors.
objective: Recognize otherwise unexplained new systolic heart failure after delivery as possible peripartum cardiomyopathy rather than normal postpartum fluid retention.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 36-year-old woman develops severe chest pressure three weeks after delivery. ECG and troponin confirm an acute coronary syndrome. She has no smoking history, diabetes or known dyslipidemia. Coronary angiography shows a long smooth narrowing in the mid-to-distal LAD with an angiographic wall contrast pattern consistent with an intramural process; other arteries have little atherosclerosis. Which mechanism should be prioritized?

options.text: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection with intramural hematoma compressing the lumen
options.explanation: A postpartum ACS with a long smooth coronary narrowing and arterial-wall abnormality supports SCAD, which can occur without the conventional atherosclerotic risk profile.

options.text: A benign musculoskeletal cause because she is young and recently delivered
options.explanation: Objective ischemic ECG changes, troponin elevation and the demonstrated coronary lesion cannot be dismissed using age or postpartum status as reassurance.

options.text: A fixed calcified atherosclerotic plaque proven solely by any narrowing
options.explanation: Coronary narrowing has multiple causes; the long smooth wall-related lesion and minimal background atherosclerosis favor a nonatherosclerotic mechanism in this clinical setting.

options.text: Isolated pericardial inflammation that directly creates the demonstrated coronary wall hematoma
options.explanation: Pericarditis does not explain the supplied intramural coronary lesion, and the angiographic process requires its own coronary diagnosis rather than a pericardial label.

explanation: SCAD involves separation within the coronary wall, often with an intramural hematoma that compresses the true lumen. It is an important cause of ACS in younger women and can occur in association with pregnancy. A low conventional risk burden therefore does not exclude serious coronary disease. The vignette supplies a compatible angiographic pattern rather than diagnosing from demographics alone. Management is not identical to routine plaque-rupture ACS and depends on stability, ongoing ischemia and anatomy. The question does not recommend invasive intracoronary imaging automatically, since instrumentation can carry added risk in a fragile vessel.
objective: Consider SCAD as a coronary arterial-wall cause of ACS in a postpartum patient with compatible nonatherosclerotic angiographic findings.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 62-year-old man has persistent chest pressure and diaphoresis for forty minutes. The standard ECG shows horizontal ST depression in V1–V3 with prominent R waves and upright T waves in those leads. Posterior leads are obtained immediately and show new ST elevation in V7–V9. He remains symptomatic. Which diagnosis best explains the relationship between these lead findings?

options.text: Isolated right ventricular hypertrophy without acute ischemia
options.explanation: Right ventricular hypertrophy may alter anterior forces but does not adequately explain new posterior ST elevation during an ongoing acute ischemic symptom syndrome.

options.text: A normal variant that makes coronary evaluation unnecessary
options.explanation: Persistent ischemic symptoms and new regional posterior ST elevation are not reassuring normal findings and require urgent acute coronary assessment.

options.text: Diffuse nonischemic pericarditis as the best match
options.explanation: The regional reciprocal anterior-posterior pattern differs from the more diffuse changes usually expected in uncomplicated pericarditis and aligns with an acute coronary territory.

options.text: Acute posterior myocardial infarction
options.explanation: Posterior injury can produce reciprocal ST depression in anterior leads, and the directly recorded posterior ST elevation supports the posterior infarction pattern.

explanation: The posterior wall is not directly represented by the usual precordial leads. Injury there can appear as reciprocal anterior ST depression with increased R-wave prominence. Recording posterior leads can show the corresponding ST elevation and prevent underrecognition of an occlusive infarction pattern. The combined ECG and ongoing symptoms are decisive; the learner should not treat all ST depression as a reason to defer urgent evaluation. This item avoids a borderline amplitude calculation and instead tests the spatial relationship between lead groups. Alternative causes of anterior changes do not account as well for the new posterior findings.
objective: Recognize posterior infarction when reciprocal anterior ST depression is accompanied by directly recorded posterior ST elevation.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 54-year-old woman arrives twenty minutes after the onset of severe central chest pressure. Her first ECG is nondiagnostic, and the initial high-sensitivity troponin is below the assay threshold. She remains pale and uncomfortable with continuing symptoms, but blood pressure and oxygenation are stable. The team is continuing an appropriate ACS evaluation. Which ECG strategy is most appropriate now?

options.text: Wait until the next annual visit before recording another ECG
options.explanation: A delayed routine appointment does not address continuing acute symptoms that may reflect a dynamic coronary event requiring immediate reassessment.

options.text: Use pain relief after an antacid as the sole replacement for repeat ECG assessment
options.explanation: Symptom response to a nonspecific treatment does not reliably exclude ischemia or replace objective reassessment when the clinical concern remains high.

options.text: Repeat 12-lead ECGs while symptoms persist and reassess for evolving ischemic changes
options.explanation: Early ischemic findings may evolve, so ongoing high-suspicion symptoms justify serial ECG assessment rather than relying on a single initial tracing.

options.text: Permanently exclude ACS because the first ECG was nondiagnostic
options.explanation: A nondiagnostic early tracing does not exclude evolving ischemia, particularly while symptoms remain active and the first biomarker was obtained soon after onset.

explanation: An ECG is a time-specific observation rather than an absolute exclusion test for every stage of ACS. Ongoing symptoms shortly after onset warrant repeat tracings because dynamic changes may appear after the first recording. The early biomarker result also needs interpretation within a validated serial pathway rather than being treated as final by itself. Serial ECGs are one component of continued emergency evaluation, not a substitute for clinical monitoring or appropriate troponin testing. New posterior or right-sided findings may require additional leads according to the evolving presentation. Waiting for a routine visit would miss the relevant diagnostic window.
objective: Obtain serial ECGs when suspected ACS remains clinically likely despite a nondiagnostic initial tracing.
keyPoints: Obtain serial ECGs when suspected ACS remains clinically likely despite a nondiagnostic initial tracing.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 67-year-old man with bacterial sepsis has high-sensitivity troponin values that rise and then fall above the assay reference limit. He has no ischemic symptoms, new ischemic ECG change or new regional wall-motion abnormality. There is no coronary thrombus evidence. A trainee writes that the biomarker pattern alone proves a type 1 myocardial infarction. Which correction is most accurate?

options.text: A rise and fall proves chronic stable injury with no acute component
options.explanation: A meaningful dynamic change supports an acute process, whereas a persistently stable elevation would be more compatible with chronic injury in the right clinical setting.

options.text: The results establish acute myocardial injury; myocardial infarction additionally requires evidence of ischemia
options.explanation: A dynamic troponin elevation identifies acute injury, but the infarction label requires an ischemic context and type 1 further implies an atherothrombotic mechanism.

options.text: Any detectable troponin proves acute plaque rupture regardless of the clinical findings
options.explanation: Troponin is not specific for plaque rupture; sepsis and other systemic illnesses can cause myocardial injury without the additional criteria for type 1 infarction.

options.text: Troponin cannot rise in sepsis, so every result must be a laboratory error
options.explanation: Systemic illness can produce real myocardial injury; dismissing the pattern as impossible is no more justified than automatically assigning an atherothrombotic diagnosis.

explanation: The universal classification distinguishes myocardial injury from infarction. Troponin above the reference limit indicates injury, and a rise or fall supports an acute component. Infarction requires additional evidence that ischemia caused the injury; type 1 infarction specifically involves an atherothrombotic process. Sepsis supplies a plausible noncoronary context, and the vignette provides no supporting ischemic finding. This does not prove that coronary disease is absent or that future ischemic symptoms should be ignored. It prevents a biomarker-only label from silently determining antithrombotic or invasive treatment without the clinical evidence needed for that classification.
objective: Distinguish acute myocardial injury from myocardial infarction by requiring evidence of ischemia in addition to dynamic troponin elevation.
keyPoints: Distinguish acute myocardial injury from myocardial infarction by requiring evidence of ischemia in addition to dynamic troponin elevation.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 63-year-old man has an acute myocardial infarction and is receiving appropriate reperfusion evaluation and other indicated therapy. He breathes comfortably on room air with repeated oxygen saturation of 97%. Lung examination is clear, blood pressure is stable and there is no shock or chronic oxygen requirement. A standing order requests oxygen for every infarction patient. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Do not add routine supplemental oxygen; continue monitoring and treat hypoxemia if it develops
options.explanation: Routine oxygen does not improve outcomes in adequately oxygenated ACS patients, while monitoring preserves the ability to respond if a separate oxygen indication emerges.

options.text: Give high-flow oxygen solely because every infarct requires hyperoxia
options.explanation: An infarction diagnosis alone does not justify routine high-flow oxygen when measured oxygenation is normal and there is no additional respiratory indication.

options.text: Withhold reperfusion treatment because normal saturation proves there is no infarction
options.explanation: Normal systemic oxygenation does not exclude coronary occlusion or myocardial ischemia; it changes the oxygen order rather than the need for appropriate acute coronary care.

options.text: Stop oxygen saturation monitoring because the first value was normal
options.explanation: Oxygenation can change during an acute event; avoiding unnecessary treatment does not remove the need to monitor and reassess the patient.

explanation: Supplemental oxygen should address a clinical oxygenation need rather than function as an automatic ritual after an infarction diagnosis. This patient has repeated normal saturation, clear lungs and no shock or separate respiratory indication. Routine oxygen therefore adds no established outcome benefit, while continued observation allows treatment if hypoxemia develops. The conclusion applies to the supplied stable oxygenation status and must not be generalized to a hypoxemic or deteriorating patient. Normal saturation also says nothing about whether coronary reperfusion is needed; coronary flow and arterial oxygen concentration are distinct parts of myocardial oxygen delivery.
objective: Avoid routine supplemental oxygen in normoxemic ACS while continuing oxygenation monitoring and other indicated treatment.
keyPoints: Avoid routine supplemental oxygen in normoxemic ACS while continuing oxygenation monitoring and other indicated treatment.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 59-year-old man underwent drug-eluting LAD stent placement ten days ago. He stopped his prescribed P2Y12 inhibitor four days later because he misunderstood the discharge instructions. He now has abrupt severe chest pain with new anterior ST elevation and diaphoresis. There is no tearing back pain or new pulse deficit. Which complication should be prioritized during his urgent coronary evaluation?

options.text: Benign postprocedural soreness requiring only reassurance
options.explanation: New regional ST elevation with severe acute symptoms is not explained by ordinary access-site or postprocedural soreness and requires emergency evaluation.

options.text: Slow in-stent restenosis as the most likely explanation for this abrupt early event
options.explanation: Restenosis generally reflects a more gradual process; the early timing, abrupt onset and medication interruption more strongly suggest thrombotic occlusion.

options.text: Proof that the original stent permanently eliminated future coronary risk
options.explanation: A coronary intervention does not remove thrombosis risk, particularly when required antiplatelet therapy is interrupted during the vulnerable early period.

options.text: Acute thrombosis of the recently implanted coronary stent
options.explanation: Very recent stenting followed by interruption of prescribed platelet inhibition and new ischemia in the treated territory makes stent thrombosis an urgent leading concern.

explanation: Stent thrombosis is a time-critical cause of recurrent ACS. The combination of a very recent implant, interrupted prescribed P2Y12 therapy and abrupt ischemia in the same territory strongly raises this concern. Urgent angiographic evaluation is needed to establish the anatomy and treat the event; the history alone is not a final angiographic diagnosis. Distinguish this from gradual restenosis or benign postprocedure discomfort. After stabilization, medication reconciliation and clear teach-back instructions matter because the interruption was a misunderstanding rather than an established contraindication. The item does not specify a universal antiplatelet duration for every future patient.
objective: Prioritize stent thrombosis when abrupt recurrent ischemia follows early interruption of prescribed antiplatelet therapy after PCI.
keyPoints: Prioritize stent thrombosis when abrupt recurrent ischemia follows early interruption of prescribed antiplatelet therapy after PCI.

subject: Medicine
stem: A 72-year-old woman is seen two weeks after PCI for an acute coronary syndrome. She is taking prescribed aspirin and a P2Y12 inhibitor. She previously had a bleeding peptic ulcer but currently has no pain, melena, anemia or active bleeding. Her cardiologist confirms that antiplatelet treatment remains indicated. Which additional medication strategy best addresses her gastrointestinal risk?

options.text: Add a daily nonselective NSAID to protect the gastric mucosa
options.explanation: Nonselective NSAIDs can increase GI injury and bleeding and do not provide gastroprotection in a patient receiving antiplatelet treatment.

options.text: Replace the P2Y12 inhibitor with an antioxidant vitamin to reduce ulcer risk
options.explanation: Antioxidant vitamins do not supply equivalent post-PCI platelet inhibition, so this substitution would sacrifice the intended antithrombotic effect without an evidence-based benefit.

options.text: Provide an appropriate proton pump inhibitor while continuing the indicated antiplatelet plan
options.explanation: A PPI is recommended for patients at risk of GI bleeding who require antiplatelet therapy; it addresses a modifiable hazard without unplanned withdrawal of needed protection.

options.text: Stop both antiplatelet agents immediately despite no active bleeding or individualized review
options.explanation: An old ulcer history warrants risk mitigation and reassessment, but abrupt unsupervised withdrawal shortly after ACS PCI may expose her to preventable thrombotic risk.

explanation: Her prior ulcer bleeding identifies a meaningful GI risk while antiplatelet treatment remains necessary. PPI gastroprotection is an appropriate mitigation strategy, with selection and interactions reviewed by the treating team. The absence of active bleeding makes this different from an acute hemorrhage requiring stabilization and a coordinated antithrombotic decision. Antiplatelet duration and intensity can be individualized, but they should not be changed automatically or without the clinician managing the recent PCI. Avoiding unnecessary NSAIDs and reviewing other bleeding hazards are complementary steps rather than alternatives to effective gastroprotection.
objective: Use appropriate PPI gastroprotection when a patient at increased GI bleeding risk requires antiplatelet therapy after ACS.
keyPoints: Use appropriate PPI gastroprotection when a patient at increased GI bleeding risk requires antiplatelet therapy after ACS.
